chunks: And from him, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad, who said:

I wrote to the latter (Imam al-Rida, peace be upon him) regarding a man who died with a debt of making up ten days from the month of Ramadan, and he had two heirs. Is it permissible for both of them to make up for him together, one of the heirs making up five days and the other heir making up five days? He replied: 'Make up for him ten days as heirs, if God wills.' There is no contradiction between these two reports and the earlier reports, because they only included the heir making up for the deceased who has a debt of making up the month of Ramadan. And whoever died in his illness, nothing is upon him, so it does not need to be made up for him, because the obligation is what became due upon him. The way to understand both is that they are applied to one who missed the month of Ramadan due to illness or otherwise, then recovered and was able to make it up, but did not make it up, then became ill and died. It becomes obligatory upon his heir to make it up for him, because the making up became obligatory upon him in the state of his ability, so he was negligent. And reports have come with this detail, some of which:

key_terms.وِلَآء: Heirship / status of being an heir

ai.seo_question: Can heirs make up the missed fasts of a deceased person who died after Ramadan?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi records this ruling in *al-Istibsar*, where the Imam resolves the apparent contradiction between reports by distinguishing between a person who dies while still incapacitated (no debt remains) and one who missed fasts, recovered, neglected them, and then died (obligation remains). This distinction highlights the Shia juristic principle that *qada* becomes a fixed debt upon the deceased's ability to perform it, making it inheritable by the heir who may fast on their behalf. The text emphasizes that the two heirs can collectively fulfill the ten days, reinforcing the flexibility in performing the make-up fasts for the deceased.
